title: American Revolution and War of Independence
summary: Thirteen British North American colonies went to war with Britain from April 1775, declared independence on 4 July 1776, won French military backing after Saratoga, and had their independence recognized in the Treaty of Paris of 3 September 1783.
card: The war began at Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775 and concluded with the Treaty of Paris on 3 September 1783. American independence was secured through major military turning points at Saratoga and Yorktown, sustained by French alliance, but the conflict also divided communities, with tens of thousands of Loyalists fleeing into exile. The struggle profoundly reshaped North America for enslaved Black people and Native nations, whose allegiances split across both sides and whose sovereign interests were ignored in the final peace settlement.
what:
The American Revolution was the political and military conflict (1775–1783) in which thirteen British North American colonies rejected British imperial rule and established the United States. Hostilities began on 19 April 1775, when British soldiers marching to seize colonial military stores clashed with provincial militia at Lexington and Concord; the American Battlefield Trust tallies 93 American and 300 British casualties. On 4 July 1776, the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence, articulating grievances against the British Crown regarding taxation, standing armies, and colonial governance.

The conflict expanded into an international war. After American forces captured General John Burgoyne's army at Saratoga in October 1777, France concluded formal treaties of alliance and commerce in February 1778, providing essential naval, financial, and troop assistance; Spain declared war on Britain in 1779. In October 1781, French naval control of the Chesapeake combined with a Franco-American siege forced Lord Cornwallis to surrender at Yorktown, where roughly 7,400 to 8,000 British, German, and Loyalist troops yielded.

The war divided populations across North America. On 7 November 1775, Virginia royal governor Lord Dunmore issued a proclamation granting freedom to enslaved people owned by rebels if they bore arms for the Crown. Thousands of Black Loyalists joined British forces in units such as the Ethiopian Regiment and Black Pioneers, while an estimated 5,000 Black soldiers served in Patriot militias and the Continental Army. In 1783, British commanders evacuated approximately 3,000 Black Loyalists from New York to Nova Scotia, recorded in the British-American inspection ledger known as the Book of Negroes. Concurrently, roughly sixty thousand white Loyalists departed into exile. Native American nations also faced bitter internal fractures: the Haudenosaunee Confederacy split, provoking the destructive 1779 Sullivan expedition that leveled 40 Haudenosaunee towns, while Cherokee fighters resisted colonial encroachment along southern frontiers.

The definitive Treaty of Paris was signed on 3 September 1783—contrasting with the Avalon Project transcript headline error giving 30 September—securing American boundaries to the Mississippi River while completely excluding Indigenous allies. Discrepancies among sources regarding prisoner counts and precise battle totals reflect differing period rosters.

uncertainty.note: Start is the opening armed conflict at Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775; the broader political crisis began in the 1760s. End is the signing of the definitive Treaty of Paris on 3 September 1783, as recorded in its signing clause and confirmed by the U.S. National Archives. The Avalon Project document header mistakenly gives 30 September 1783, but its concluding text gives the third day of September.

how: The immediate cause of the fighting was a British attempt to disarm Massachusetts after the Coercive Acts. Governor Gage sent troops to seize arms stored at Concord; riders such as Paul Revere warned the countryside, and militia gathered at Lexington and fought the column along its route back to Boston. The colonies then formed a Continental Army and in 1776 declared independence. Burgoyne's advance down the Hudson valley ended in his army's surrender at Saratoga in October 1777. Saratoga convinced the French court that the colonists would persist, and the 1778 treaties of alliance and commerce followed; France provided supplies, troops and naval support, and the treaty barred either party from making a separate peace with Britain. In 1781 Cornwallis, based at Yorktown, was cut off when a French fleet held the entrance to Chesapeake Bay, and Washington and Rochambeau besieged him with over 18,000 allied troops. His surrender led to a preliminary agreement in 1782 and the definitive treaty in 1783.
why_it_matters: The war created the United States and produced, in the Declaration of Independence, a written case for breaking with a monarch that later movements could cite. The Treaty of Paris recognized the new states and set their western boundary at the Mississippi River, which drew the line for settlement into an interior where Native nations lived: the Haudenosaunee Confederacy had already been broken apart by the war, and the Oneida, who sided with the United States, were eventually left on a 32-acre reservation after later New York land purchases. The war also exposed the contradiction between liberty and slavery. Dunmore's Proclamation and later British offers pushed enslaved people to flee, and about 3,000 Black Loyalists were evacuated from New York to Nova Scotia in 1783, yet slavery remained legal in the new republic. Without Saratoga and the French alliance, the Americans would have lacked the fleet that trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown, and independence might have come later or on different terms. Had Britain been able to hold the Chesapeake in 1781, the surrender that ended the main fighting could not have happened as it did.

perspectives.holder: American Patriots as stated in the Declaration of Independence
perspectives.account: The Declaration presents the break as a necessary response to persistent abuses by King George III, including taxation without consent, peacetime standing armies, interference with colonial assemblies, and the employment of foreign mercenaries against colonial subjects.

Loyalists, who made up an estimated 15 to 20 percent of white colonists and came from all social ranks, viewed armed rebellion as unlawful treason that undermined the British constitutional order; tens of thousands suffered confiscation of property, social ostracism, and violent reprisals, with roughly sixty thousand fleeing into exile to Canada, Britain, and the Caribbean.

African Americans pursued freedom by navigating both sides of the conflict. While an estimated 5,000 served with American forces seeking personal liberty or civic equality, thousands more seized British offers of freedom—beginning with Lord Dunmore's 7 November 1775 proclamation—joining units like the Ethiopian Regiment and Black Pioneers, resulting in the 1783 evacuation of roughly 3,000 Black Loyalists recorded in the Book of Negroes.

Native nations fought primarily to defend their territorial sovereignty against colonial encroachment. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy suffered a painful civil split, with Mohawks, Senecas, Cayugas, and Onondagas largely allying with Britain and Oneidas and Tuscaroras supporting Americans; this brought total war, notably the 1779 Sullivan expedition destroying 40 towns. In the South, Cherokee fighters attacked encroaching settlements in 1776 but saw their towns ravaged in retaliation. In the 1783 Treaty of Paris, Britain ceded all claims to trans-Appalachian Indigenous homelands to the United States without consulting or providing for their Native allies, leaving both British-allied and American-allied nations dispossessed.

audience_note: The record describes warfare, military casualties, the flight and emancipation struggles of enslaved people, property confiscation and exile of Loyalists, and the destruction of Haudenosaunee and Cherokee towns and crops.

importance.justification: It established the United States as an independent constitutional republic and profoundly transformed imperial governance, trans-Atlantic politics, slavery, and Indigenous territories across North America.

reviewer_note: Coordinator review: Yorktown surrender corrected to the cited almost 8,000; Loyalist exile figure (60,000) removed as not on its cited page. Least sure of eighteenth-century troop tallies and casualty figures due to conflicting rosters and retrospective estimates across sources.
